Essentials of Cultivation and Realization
Cultivation
: follow the manifest stream of one's own mind and purify away the habits of deluded thought.
Realization: when a single deluded thought suddenly ceases, one sees through to the fundamental nature.
[Manifest stream of one's own mind] The present stream of thoughts as it manifests.

When speaking of this great matter of causes and conditions (to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision), although it is inherent in every person, complete in each of us, lacking not a hair's breadth, yet from beginningless kalpas the habit seeds of craving and desire, deluded thoughts and emotional rumination, and deeply ingrained defilements have veiled the wondrous, clear true mind, so that we gain no true benefit from it. All along we have been toiling within the shadow of delusion that is body, mind, and world, and thus we have wandered through birth and death. When the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world, their thousands upon thousands of words and all manner of skillful means — whether teaching Chan or expounding doctrine — were nothing more than instruments suited to the occasion for breaking through beings' attachment to self and attachment to phenomena; they never gave people any real dharma.

What is called cultivation is merely following the manifest stream of one's own mind and purifying away the habits of deluded thought and of greed, anger, and ignorance. To apply effort here is what is called cultivation. If one cultivates in this down-to-earth way, and a single deluded thought suddenly ceases, one directly sees that one's own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast and great, pure in its very essence, with not a single thing in it — this is what is called realization. There is nothing beyond this mind that can be cultivated or realized. For the essence of the mind is like a mirror, while the shadows of delusion and clinging are the dust upon the true mind. Thus it is said that the characteristics of thought are dust, and the feelings of consciousness are grime. When deluded thoughts melt away, the original essence appears of itself. It is like polishing a bronze mirror: when the dust and grime are wiped clean, the mirror's body is fully revealed and its light shines forth. It is naturally so.
[Naturally so] Meaning natural, spontaneous, not awaiting contrivance.

But the defilements and habits we have accumulated over beginningless kalpas are solid and firm, and the root of self-cherishing runs so deep it is hard to pull out. In this life we are fortunate to have our inherent prajñā inwardly perfuming us as the cause, and outwardly a good spiritual friend to draw it forth as the condition; thus we come to know our own fundamental nature and resolve with determination to escape birth and death. Yet to uproot at a single stroke the root of birth and death accumulated over countless kalpas — how could this be a small matter? Unless one is a person of great strength who shoulders the burden with full resolve and charges straight in, to escape birth and death is indeed difficult beyond all difficulty. The ancients said: to escape birth and death is like one man battling ten thousand. These are no idle words!

Generally speaking, in this age of the declining Dharma, many people practice, but few gain true benefit; many exert themselves, but few gain strength. Why is this? It is because they do not apply their effort at the direct point of entry, but instead use the feelings of consciousness to speculate on the experiences, intellectual understandings, and words of their predecessors, suppressing deluded thoughts and working only at the threshold of light and shadow. They always first store up the ancients' abstruse words and subtle phrases in their breast, taking them for real Dharma (mistaking the finger that points at the moon for the moon itself) and regarding them as their own knowledge and views (this is learned understanding, not understanding won through realization, and so it is not truly their own). Little do they realize that in cultivation and realization these intellectual interpretations and abstruse words are of
no use at all
— this is precisely what is meant by “relying on another's explanation to plug up the gate of one's own awakening.”

Now, in doing the work, one must first shovel away intellectual understanding and work purely and simply upon the single thought alone. Truly believe that one's own mind is originally spotless and clean, with not a thread attached to it, perfectly clear and bright, pervading the entire Dharma realm. Originally there is no body, no mind, no world, and no deluded thoughts or emotional rumination. This very thought is originally unborn. The various states that appear before one now are all illusory and unreal, nothing but shadows manifested within the true mind.

Once you have seen through it in this way, then at the very place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze firmly with a single glance. Watch it: from where does it arise, and toward where does it cease? (This is the method of contemplating the mind spoken of later.) Press hard in this way with a single thrust (zǎn,
to squeeze or press

), and no matter what kind of deluded thought it is, one thrust will shatter it and it will vanish on the spot. You must never follow it (the deluded thought) as it flows on, nor allow it to continue — this is what Master Yongjia meant by cutting off the mind of continuity.

Because deluded thoughts are originally without root, you must never take them for real things and lodge them in your breast. The moment a deluded thought arises, give a shout — “Duo!” — and the instant you shout, it disappears. Never try to suppress your thoughts, or you will be dragged along by them, like gourds on the water: press one down and another bobs up, endlessly, without end. Simply cast body, mind, and world aside, and purely raise this one thought (watch from where the deluded thought arises and toward where it ceases — or, the moment a thought arises, give a shout). Like a sword stretched across the sky, whether it be Buddha (a wholesome thought) or demon (an unwholesome thought), cut them all off together, like slashing through tangled silk. Press hard upon deluded thoughts with utter urgency; this state in which the deluded thought has nowhere to hide is the direct mind rightly mindful of suchness. (Layman Pang said: “Simply look at the place where it arises and ceases — this very thing is suchness.”) Right mindfulness is no-mind. To be able to contemplate no-mind may be called advancing toward the Buddha's wisdom.

At the very outset of practice, in arousing the mind, one must truly believe in the Dharma gate of mind-only. The Buddha said: the three realms are mind alone; the myriad dharmas are consciousness only. So much of the Buddhadharma is merely an explanation of these eight characters, clarifying the principle within them so that everyone may come to believe. In sum, the two paths of sage and ordinary being are merely the two paths of delusion and awakening within one's own mind. Apart from this mind, not a single thing can be grasped in all good and evil, cause and effect. For our wondrous nature is natural and spontaneous — originally it does not belong to awakening, so how could it ever be deluded

Now when we speak of delusion, it is only that one does not understand that one's own mind originally contains not a single thing, and has not realized that body, mind, and world are originally empty; being obstructed by them, we call it delusion. Because one has always used only the deluded, arising-and-ceasing mind to think and calculate, and taken it for real, one regards the various illusory transformations of the six sense-objects and conditions as actually existing.

Now, in resolving to escape birth and death, this is the supreme upward step of turning back the flow to return to the source. One must entirely cast off all one's former intellectual understanding, making no use whatsoever of any knowledge, views, or clever methods. Simply see through at a single glance this present body, mind, and world of yours — all of it is floating light and illusory shadow manifested within one's own mind, like images in a mirror, like the moon in water. Contemplate all sounds as wind passing through the trees; contemplate all states as clouds drifting across the sky; all are changing, illusory, unreal things. Not only are external states thus, but even the deluded thoughts and emotional rumination of one's own mind — all the seeds of craving, all habitual defilements — are likewise floating, illusory, unreal. One must contemplate deeply in this way.

Whenever a single thought arises, you must investigate where it lands — watch from where it arises and toward where it ceases. Never let it slip by lightly, nor be deceived by it and fall into deluded thinking. To do the work in this way is to draw somewhat near to true earnestness. Beyond this, to drag in various abstruse views and clever methods to piece things together is entirely beside the point. Even the very mention of “doing the work” is itself a matter of having no choice. It is like the use of arms: weapons are instruments of ill omen, employed only when there is no alternative. When the ancients spoke of investigating Chan and raising the huatou, it was likewise only because they had no other way. Although the gong'ans are many, only the huatou that investigates Buddha-recitation — “Who is reciting the Buddha's name?” — is most effective amid affliction. Yet although it is easily effective, it is after all no more than a door-knocking
brick
— ultimately to be thrown away; it is only at the beginning that one cannot do without making use of it for a while.

Now, in using this huatou (“Who is reciting the Buddha's name?”) to do the work, you must be able to believe it through, to rely on it firmly, to bite down on it and hold fast, and never to waver. Do not do it one way today and another way tomorrow; do not fear that you will fail to awaken, nor despise it as insufficiently profound. All such deliberation and calculation are obstructions, so I am telling you this in advance, that when the time comes you will not give rise to doubt.

If the work is done to the point where it gains strength, external states no longer enter, and only the afflictions within the mind flare up on their own, suddenly and without cause. Perhaps desire erupts at random, or the mind grows restless and depressed, or all manner of obstructions arise, until the mind is weary and exhausted, with nothing left to do. These are the habit seeds accumulated over countless kalpas that are stored within the ālaya consciousness, now driven out into the open because the work has pressed them hard. This is the most critical juncture, and you must know it clearly in your own mind: first you must see through them and pass through them, and you must never let them envelop you, never let them toy with you, never take them for real things. Only rouse your spirit, press forward with fierce courage, and raise the huatou you are investigating (“Who is reciting the Buddha's name?”). If the afflictions of desire still linger and will not leave, then at the very place where those thoughts arise, pursue them relentlessly: here in me originally there is no such thing — ask it, from where did it come? What is it, after all? You must see where it lands. Pressing down in this way, you will make even ghosts and spirits weep, and they will vanish without a trace. You must drive them out to the last and spare not a single thread. Applying such effort, you will naturally come upon good news.

If a single thought is pressed through and broken, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like flowers in the sky fading, like the shimmering waves of a mirage growing still. Once past this pass, one attains boundless ease and boundless freedom. This is where beginners gain strength, and it should not be regarded as something profound. As for the ease and freedom themselves, one must not give rise to a mind of delight. If a mind of delight arises, the demon of delight attaches to the mind, and there is one more obstruction.

If the habit seeds and the seeds of craving within the ālaya consciousness are solid and deeply hidden, then at such a time investigating the huatou gains no strength and contemplating the mind sheds no light upon them, and one cannot find a way to begin. One must then pay homage to the Buddha, recite sutras, repent, and also secretly uphold the mantra-heart, relying on the Buddha's secret seal to eradicate them. For all the secret mantras are the vajra heart-seals of the Buddhas. When we recite and hold the mantra-heart, it is like holding a vajra jeweled club in hand: whatever it meets, it shatters to fine dust. The secret essentials of the heart-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old all come down to nothing other than this. Hence it is said: “The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by upholding this mantra-heart, attained supreme perfect enlightenment.” However, the Buddha openly declared this to beings, while the Patriarchs, fearing that it might fall into ordinary sentiment, kept it secret and did not speak of it — not that they did not use it. In secretly upholding the mantra-heart one must have a fixed daily practice; with long familiarity it ripens and gains great strength, but one must not hope for miraculous responses.

Among practitioners there are those who awaken first and cultivate afterward (sudden awakening, gradual cultivation) and those who cultivate first and awaken afterward (gradual cultivation, sudden awakening); accordingly, awakening is divided into awakening through understanding and awakening through realization. If one realizes the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, this is awakening through understanding. Those who awaken through understanding mostly fall into intellectual views and gain little strength amid all states and conditions. This is because mind and object still stand in opposition and have not yet merged; thus, when meeting objects and conditions, one is pulled and entangled, with many obstructions. This is semblance prajñā, not genuine investigation. But one who awakens through realization works on steadfastly from within one's own mind (through the work of contemplating the mind or of Chan investigation), pressing hard until the water runs dry and the mountains come to an end, when suddenly a single
subtle thought

ceases and one thoroughly realizes one's own mind — like meeting one's own father at a crossroads and recognizing him at a single glance, with no doubt as to whether it is he. This state is like a person drinking water: only the drinker knows whether it is cold or warm, and it cannot be conveyed to another. Only this is genuine investigation and true realization. Then, using this point of realization, one merges mind and object, purifies away the present karmic flow of consciousness, and melts all deluded thoughts and emotional rumination into the single flavor of the true mind — this is realization.

This realization also differs in depth and shallowness. If one does the work from the root (working purely and simply on the single thought alone), breaking through the lair of the eight consciousnesses and instantly overturning the den of ignorance, one leaps straight through at a single bound, with no dharma left over. For people of the highest and sharpest faculties, what is realized is deep; for the rest, in gradual cultivation, what is realized is shallow. What is most to be feared is being satisfied with a little; one must never sink into the threshold of light and shadow and take it for the ultimate, and so advance no further. Why? Because the fundamental ignorance of the eight consciousnesses has not yet been broken, and however much one may accomplish, it all remains a matter of the spirit of consciousness (the consciousness-mind). If one takes this for the true, it is exactly like mistaking a thief for one's own son. The ancients said: “The student of the Way fails to know the true, because all along he has known the spirit of consciousness; the root of birth and death over countless kalpas (the very root of birth and death), the fool mistakes for the original person.” This pass of sinking into the threshold of light and shadow must be thoroughly passed through.

What is meant by sudden awakening and gradual cultivation is this: one has already thoroughly awakened, but habits still remain and cannot be purified all at once. Thus, amid all states and conditions, using the principle one has realized, one arouses the power of contemplative insight, passing through states to test the mind. Merge with one fraction of a state, and one realizes one fraction of the dharmakāya; dissolve one fraction of delusion, and one reveals one fraction of fundamental wisdom. All of this, again, is accomplished through continuous, meticulous work amid states, and is therefore all the more effective.

Those of sharp faculties and courageous faith are all willing to put in hard work in their practice; their obstructions of phenomena are easy to remove, but their obstructions of principle are hard to dispel. A few of the ailments involved are briefly enumerated below.
First, do not crave the profound and wondrous.

Because this matter is from the start perfectly plain and even, solid and down-to-earth, wholly ordinary, with nothing profound about it at all. Hence the ancients said: “After awakening one is the same as before awakening — still the same old person (not increased by a hair's breadth) — yet not treading the same old path (after awakening the eyes are clear and keen, no longer deceived by seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, so that in meeting states and conditions one handles them differently than before, no longer clinging to appearances).” Therefore there is nothing profound about it. If the work is brought to maturity, it is naturally plain and solid. But because our habits of intellectual understanding are not yet pure, and inwardly perfume the prajñā, the prajñā, perfumed by the habits of intellectual understanding, is measured and weighed by the feelings of consciousness, giving rise to many illusions and producing all kinds of false, profound-seeming views that wrap and bind the mind. Yet one takes them for the profound, and clings to them deeply, unwilling to let go. How could one know that this is precisely the shadowy brightness of the spirit of consciousness, the root of discriminating false views, also called the thorn of views? It differs from the earlier coarse and superficial deluded thoughts; this is the subtle flowing stream of arising and ceasing, also called the obstruction of knowledge, and it is precisely what obstructs right understanding. If one mistakes it and takes it for a true state, all manner of arrogant views arise. This is what practice most forbids.
Second, do not set your mind to wait for awakening.

Because our wondrous, perfect true mind is originally absolute and beyond all comparison. All along, because delusion has congealed, mind and object, sense-roots and sense-objects, stand opposed to one another, and so confusion arises and karma is created. Now, in practicing, one does the work solely on the single thought. Set down body, mind, and world, and purely raise this one thought (contemplating the mind or investigating Chan) and press forward; pay no heed to whether there is awakening or not, and simply keep doing it thought by thought, step by step. If the work is brought to maturity, one will naturally see the original face; what need is there to calculate in advance? If one sets one's mind to wait for awakening, then this very mind that waits for awakening is the root of birth and death. Waiting in this way until the year of the donkey or the month of the horse, one will never awaken. This is because one does not understand the absolute true mind, and still imagines there is something else beyond it. If the mind that waits for awakening is not removed, weariness and aversion easily arise and one mostly falls into retreat. It is like searching for a thing and, failing to find it, giving rise to the thought of giving up.
Third, do not hope for wondrous fruit.

Because the deluded mind of birth and death in living beings is itself, from the very beginning, the body of the Buddha's fruition. (When the self-nature is deluded, one is a living being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.) Now, because the self-nature is deluded, the spiritual powers and wondrous functions of all Buddhas are turned into deluded thoughts, emotional rumination, and discriminating views; the true, pure dharmakāya is turned into the karmic substance of birth and death; and the pure, wondrous land is turned into the realm of the six sense-objects. Now, in doing the work, if a single thought suddenly realizes one's own mind, it is like the great blazing furnace of creation, smelting and molding the myriad forms. This very body, mind, and world are from the start the body of the Buddha's fruition; these very deluded thoughts and emotional rumination are from the start the spiritual powers and wondrous functions — the name changes but the essence does not. As Master Yongjia's Song of Enlightenment says: “The true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is itself the dharmakāya.” If one can realize this Dharma gate, then the feelings of choosing and rejecting are forgotten and the mind of craving and aversion comes to rest; every step is the Pure Land of the Lotus Treasury, and every thought is the descent of Maitreya (the attainment of Buddhahood). If, on the contrary, one sets one's mind on craving wondrous fruit in advance, then this very mind of craving is the root of birth and death, obstructing right understanding. The more one craves wondrous fruit, the farther one is from realizing the Way; and when the craving goes unfulfilled and one's strength is exhausted, weariness and aversion arise.
Fourth, do not give rise to doubt.

Whenever one does the work, the moment one sets down body and mind and cuts off seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing, then, having already left the familiar old road and looking ahead on the new road, one finds it strange and boundless, with no place to settle one's body and establish one's life. Ahead there is no new realization, and behind one has lost the old dwelling. In such circumstances, if one plans and frets over what lies before and behind, doubt arises. Then one gives rise to endless calculations, weighing gains and losses. Or one gives rise to subjective views and sets in motion deviant thoughts, obstructing right understanding. This point must be seen through, and one must resolutely enter straight in, with no more hesitation. Generally speaking, when the work reaches the point where one can no longer go on, that is precisely where it gains strength; one should all the more rouse one's spirit and keep going. In this way one will not retreat or shrink back. Otherwise, one falls into the demon of melancholy.
Fifth, do not give rise to a mind of terror.

When the power of mindfulness in the work grows urgent, pressing down until a single deluded thought suddenly ceases, suddenly body and mind drop away into emptiness, and one sees that the great earth has not an inch of ground, deep to the ultimate — then great terror arises. If one does not see through this state, one will not dare to press forward. Or one may take this vast, open emptiness (where everything is empty) for a sublime, wondrous state. If one takes this emptiness for a sublime, wondrous state, then a great wrong view arises, and one no longer believes in cause and effect — this is the most dangerous pass.
Sixth, firmly believe that one's own mind is Buddha.

Yet there is no Buddha other than this — one's own mind is the Buddha. For the Buddha's true dharmakāya is like empty space. If one realizes that deluded thoughts are from the start illusory, then the originally existing dharmakāya appears of itself — luminous, silently illuminating, perfect, all-pervading, lacking nothing and having nothing in excess. All the more, one must not send the mind outward in pursuit; if one abandons this mind and seeks elsewhere, the mind will conjure up all manner of limitless dreamlike states. These are precisely the phantoms manifested by the spirit of consciousness, and one must never regard them as extraordinary. Know that in this pure mind of mine there is originally not a single thing, and still less a single thought. The moment a thought arises and the mind stirs, one has departed from the essence of the Dharma.
Seventh, know that deluded thoughts are from the start illusory.

Practitioners doing the work nowadays all fail to realize that the deluded thoughts of their own mind are from the start illusory. They mistake these deluded thoughts for something real and set themselves exclusively against them. This is like a child playing with lamplight shadows: the more it plays, the more irrelevant it becomes, and after playing long enough, the child itself is frightened by the shadows. (That is to say: if one mistakes deluded thoughts for real and opposes them, it is like a child toying with its own shadow cast on the wall; far from quelling the deluded thoughts, it makes them stranger and stranger, until after a long time one takes them for demons and grows afraid.) There is also a kind of person who fears deluded thoughts and wishes he could seize them in one grasp and fling them aside. This is like chasing the wind and clutching at shadows — wrestling with them all day long, exhausting every ounce of strength, without a single moment of rest. Entangled in this way for a long time, one's faith grows ever more weary, and then one says that Chan investigation has no efficacy, giving rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of fear, or a mind of retreat. This is the common ailment of beginners. There is no other reason for it: it is all because one has not realized that the abiding true mind is unborn and unceasing, and instead takes deluded thoughts for real dharma. This point must be thoroughly passed through; if one can pass through this pass, the upward road lies open of itself.
Eighth, one must investigate apart from the mind-consciousness, and seek apart from the realm of deluded thought.

Whenever a single thought arises, whether wholesome or unwholesome, cast it aside on the spot and by no means oppose it. Truly believe that in your own mind there is originally no such thing, and simply raise the huatou you are investigating with full force, like a vajra sword — when a demon (an unwholesome thought) comes, the demon is cut down; when a Buddha (a wholesome thought) comes, the Buddha is cut down. Here one most needs great valor, great vigor, and great tenacity. You must never deliberate over what lies before or behind, never be timid or hesitant. Only with a direct mind and right mindfulness, stand up straight and press forward, and you will naturally be lofty and majestic, no longer entangled by these deluded thoughts, like an eagle freed from its jesses (gōu

the leather sleeve worn on the arm in ancient archery), flying freely. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, amid all states and conditions, one is naturally no longer pulled or hindered, and naturally attains great ease and great freedom. This is where the first step of a beginner's work gains strength.

The several points set out above are, frankly, like drawing legs on a snake — merely words of expedience for the moment. They are not the ultimate, nor are they real dharma. Because you have already set out on the road, I feared only that you might take a wrong step as you go out the door, stray onto a deviant path, waste your mental effort, and squander your time, so I could not help speaking these words. In practice, one must walk a true road to Buddhahood. If the road is right and the method is right, then the swiftness of one's progress is such that what originally required a great kalpa can now be reached in a single day. In short, the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' upward road is not a matter of having to travel a great distance or spend a long time before one can realize the fruit. This principle, too, must be understood by beginners at the very outset of their journey.
